summaries.example: Imagine a playground where one older child can decide who may use the only swing, and no rule or teacher can stop that child. Even if the child does not block anyone today, the younger children may still have to act carefully because the child could do so whenever they wanted. Philosophers ask whether this kind of unchecked power counts as domination, and whether fair rules or shared decision-making would change the situation.
summaries.summary: Domination is a philosophical name for a serious kind of unfair social power. It happens when a person, group, or possibly a whole system can control important parts of another person’s life without enough checks. Slavery, tyranny, and patriarchal societies are often used as clearest examples, but domination may also appear in less extreme situations. A boss who can fire someone at will, a group that can push someone out, or a custom that gives one group more authority may raise similar questions. One debate asks who or what can dominate. Some philosophers say only people or organized groups can do this. Others say that systems, laws, markets, or social rules can themselves be sites of domination. Another debate asks whether domination requires harmful action now. Some theories focus on a person’s capacity to interfere, while others require actual interference, abuse, or a harmful result. A final debate concerns what makes power wrong: lack of limits, unequal status, unfair rules, denied rights, or failure to respect people as equal participants. The entry presents these disagreements without treating one answer as settled.
key_ideas: Domination is usually an unfair power relationship between people or groups.
A person can be dominated even when the powerful person is not using their power right now. The important question may be what that person could do.
Domination can happen in different amounts. Someone does not need complete control for their power to be troubling.
Philosophers disagree about whether only people and organized groups can dominate, or whether laws, customs, workplaces, and other systems can dominate too.
Fair rules, protection, and a real chance to have a say can limit domination, but philosophers disagree about exactly what counts as a sufficient limit.
summaries.why_it_matters: Thinking about domination helps us notice unfairness that is bigger than one unkind action. It asks who can make rules, who must obey, who can safely disagree, and who is left unable to resist. These questions matter in families, schools, workplaces, governments, medical care, and online spaces. Understanding domination can help people look for protections and ways to share power more fairly.

important_terms.definition: Power in relationships between people or groups. It is not just being strong; it is being able to shape what others can do.
A serious kind of unfair power that leaves others vulnerable and unable to protect their choices.
Power that is not properly limited by rules, shared decisions, or the interests of the people affected.
A group that is organized and able to act together, rather than merely a crowd that could possibly act together.
Shared expectations and rules that influence how people treat one another and what seems acceptable.

questions_to_think_about: Is it unfair if someone could control your choices but chooses not to?
What makes a group a real acting group instead of just many separate people?
Can a rule or custom be unfair even when no single person is in charge?
When does help from a caregiver become unfair control?
How can people make sure that power is checked?

summaries.example: Consider an employer who may dismiss a worker without having to explain the decision or follow a dependable procedure. The worker keeps the job, and the employer never threatens them. One view says the worker is already dominated because the employer has unchecked discretionary power: the worker must plan around what the employer could do. Another view asks whether the power is actually exercised, whether the worker can leave easily, whether workplace rules constrain the employer, and whether the relationship gives the employer an authority claim over the worker. The disagreement shows why domination cannot be identified simply by observing one harmful act.
summaries.summary: The entry surveys competing theories of domination, beginning from a shared but incomplete idea: domination is a morally serious form of social power in which an agent or system can determine another person’s choices or conditions without adequate constraint. The paradigms of slavery, tyranny, and patriarchy matter because a theory must explain why these relations are dominating, while also explaining less extreme cases. One axis of disagreement concerns the possible dominators. Neorepublican approaches usually treat domination as a relation among agents, including organized group agents. This raises the coalition problem: if any people who could combine count as a dominating group, domination becomes nearly universal. Concepts such as group agency and latent teams attempt to identify meaningful capacities for coordination. Other approaches give institutions, markets, ideologies, and norms a more direct role. A second axis concerns exercise. Capacity-based theories say domination lies in the structure of power and can persist without present interference; critics argue that this overgeneralizes and neglects outcomes, abuse, history, and the character of the powerful. A third axis concerns the type of power involved. Non-moralized theories may focus on uncontrolled choice interference or imposition. Moralized theories may require wrongful interference, violated interests, or impunity. Norm-dependent theories connect domination to socially recognized authority or legitimating norms, while moralized norm-dependent theories emphasize equal status, rights, and people’s authority to participate in shaping the rules that govern them. The entry presents these as rival tools for understanding different forms of injustice rather than as one settled definition.
key_ideas: The basic idea links domination with unjust, asymmetric, and insufficiently constrained social power. The paradigmatic cases include slavery, tyranny, and patriarchy, but domination can come in degrees.

A central neorepublican claim is that vulnerability to possible interference can compromise freedom. This is often called a robustness requirement: a person should be protected not only from actual interference but also from relevant possible interference.

The coalition problem challenges accounts based on what groups could do. If any collection of people counts as a dominating group, everyone may be dominated by some possible coalition. Theories of group agency or latent teams try to distinguish serious collective power from mere possibility.

A major dispute concerns the location of domination. Dyadic theories place it in relations between specific agents or organized groups; structural theories locate it partly in institutions, markets, laws, ideologies, or social norms.

Another dispute concerns whether domination requires actual exercise of power, harmful outcomes, or bad character. Capacity-based accounts emphasize power’s structure, while critics worry that they make ordinary strength, care, or persuasion look dominating.

Theories also differ over whether domination is non-moralized or moralized, and norm-independent or norm-dependent. These combinations produce different explanations in terms of unchecked choice interference, wrongs, authority, status, rights, or equal participation in justification.
summaries.why_it_matters: The concept of domination broadens political analysis beyond visible acts of coercion. It directs attention to background conditions: who can exit a relationship, who can contest decisions, whose status is recognized, which groups are protected, and how institutions shape available choices. These questions apply to employment, care, disability, migration, medicine, digital life, markets, and relations between present and future people. The disagreements matter because different definitions identify different victims and recommend different remedies, such as public rules, democratic control, legal sanctions, transformed social norms, or greater equality of status.

important_terms.definition: Social power that is unjustly or illegitimately uncontrolled and enables an agent or system to shape another person’s options or conditions of action.
A relation in which one party depends on another’s discretionary capacity to interfere, even if interference does not occur.
The ability to act intentionally on the basis of beliefs, desires, and intentions; some theories say domination requires such agents.
A coordinated entity whose members share enough beliefs, attitudes, and intentions to act together as one agent.
A group that is ready or able to coordinate in a particular setting, even without a fully organized plan; this idea helps explain vulnerability to groups.
The view that institutions, systems, and ideologies enable domination by agents but do not themselves dominate.
A theory that defines domination partly through social rules, accepted authority, or norms, rather than through power alone.
A theory that identifies domination without building moral rightness or wrongness into the definition, even though the theory may be motivated by ethical concerns.

questions_to_think_about: Does an unexercised ability to interfere threaten freedom in the same way as actual interference?
How should a theory distinguish an organized group from a merely possible coalition?
Can a market, law, or social norm dominate, or do such structures only enable particular agents to dominate?
Would dependable legal rules reduce domination even if the less powerful group did not help create those rules?
Which is more fundamental: protection from interference, equal social status, or the right to participate in making the rules?

summaries.example: Suppose a school’s debate club has a popular group that can make another student leave. The group has not planned this together, but everyone knows that if one member starts mocking the student, several others will join. The student may avoid speaking even when nobody is mocking them. Philosophers might ask whether the group is an organized agent, a ready-to-act team, or only a collection of individuals. They might also ask whether the school’s rules and social habits make the student especially vulnerable. The example shows why domination is about more than what happens at one moment.
summaries.summary: Domination is a term philosophers use for a serious kind of unfair social power. The basic idea is that one person, group, or system can shape another person’s choices or living conditions without sufficient limits. The clearest examples are slavery, tyranny, and patriarchy, but theorists also study workplaces, families, governments, markets, and other relationships. Domination can come in degrees, so complete control is not required. One important disagreement concerns unexercised power. Neorepublican theories often say that a person is unfree when another has the unchecked ability to interfere, even if the interference never happens. Critics worry that this definition could label ordinary abilities—such as physical strength, persuasion, or caregiving—as domination. Another disagreement asks who can dominate. Some theories focus on individuals and organized groups. But if any group that might join together counts, domination could become unavoidable; this is the coalition problem. Ideas such as group agency and latent teams try to separate realistic collective power from a merely imaginable group. Other philosophers argue that social structures, institutions, markets, ideologies, and norms should be treated as more than background conditions. Theories also differ over whether domination is defined without moral concepts, through actual wrongdoing, or through socially recognized authority and unequal status. The entry maps these disagreements rather than choosing one final answer.
key_ideas: Domination is usually understood as a serious injustice involving social power, not simply bad luck, weather, or illness.
It can be partial. A person may be dominated without another person having total control over every part of their life.
Some philosophers focus on the power someone has available, even when they do not use it. This protects people against threats that remain in the background.
Groups create difficult cases. A crowd is not automatically a group agent, but a group may have shared plans or a well-understood ability to coordinate.

Structural theories emphasize that laws, institutions, markets, ideologies, and social norms can shape people’s choices and status. Other theories say these things only make interpersonal domination possible.
Philosophers disagree about whether domination is best explained by lack of control, actual harm, unequal status, wrongful power, or authority supported by social norms.
summaries.why_it_matters: Studying domination helps us see how freedom and equality can be limited even when no one is openly giving orders. It encourages questions about who can make decisions, who can challenge them, who has a safe way to leave, and whose voice counts. This is useful for thinking about school rules, family responsibilities, employment, public institutions, disability, migration, online platforms, and social hierarchies. It also shows why different understandings of injustice can lead to different solutions.

important_terms.definition: Unfair social power that lets a person, group, or system control another person’s choices or situation without adequate checks.
Power that can be used according to the powerful person’s choice, without dependable limits or accountability to those affected.
The ability to make deliberate choices and act on beliefs and desires; some theories limit domination to relations among agents.
A group organized enough to have shared intentions and act together, not merely a number of people who might happen to cooperate.
A group that can coordinate in a particular situation because its members already understand how others are likely to respond.
The difficulty that arises when every possible group of people could combine to block someone’s actions, making domination seem unavoidable.
The idea that systems and institutions help agents dominate but are not themselves the dominators.
A theory that says domination involves power connected to accepted rules, authority, or social expectations.

questions_to_think_about: Should a person feel free if someone else could interfere but probably will not?
What facts would show that a group is ready to act together?
Can school rules reduce domination even if students do not directly control the school?
How might a social norm give one group authority over another?
Could a caring relationship still contain domination? What would make the answer yes or no?
